AN INTERVIEW WITH
MR. GIL EVANS
FOR
SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
PERFORMING ARTS
AMTRAK BUILDING
L'ENFANT PLAZA
Helen Armstead
This is (Sally Nonstead?) Johnston and I'm here in West Beth in New York with Gil Evans and his perfectly delightful wife Anita.

........arranging, maybe you all know, didn't pay me any money. Because arranging, you don't get any royalties from arranging. And now for a short time after you know, we go for long periods of time with no income and this all has to do with the fact that I was always an arranger of other people's music. We get tired of it sometimes and some days.
Well if that is the reason then maybe you're grumpy not only today but a number of days, on a number of days. (LAUGHTER).
(LAUGHTER)
But anyway, I would say that you have a very charming way of being grumpy. (LAUGHTER). Is there any direction that you could take

Oh, I would start, now I just write my own music. I like arranging for other people, but I haven't done much composing. I always enjoyed writing. Arranging from other people's tunes, it turned out it was a losing game. I didn't know a thing about playing.
Well, what about playing the piano?
Oh I really never have played the piano. Just for my own group. Every once in a while I have, but it was not even much you know. It wasn't my forte.
I went from highschool to see you do it at Bird Land on Basin Street somewhere. Gerry Mulligan Jerry Logan and, and something. I remember that
That's the first time ...
You mean to tell me that Gil was the attraction for you at that point too?
(LAUGHTER).
No, as a matter of fact no. I was put out because I thought somebody else was going to be on the piano. (LAUGHTER). But he turned out to be good. (LAUGHTER).
Well I think better than that, he turned out to be your husband.
(LAUGHTER).
Oh yes, but years later.
I met her later through Bud Powell
Oh?

That's when Bud Powell sent Anita a birthday tape and she didn't have a tape player. So, through a mutual friend she came to my house to play the tape and we were engaged and married immediately. (Imagine that?)?
And I met Bud in Paris, right?
She met Bud in Paris.
And what were you doing in Paris?
Ah, on vacation, kind of.
chartered plane, she came.
charter - cheap flight.
School.
Through the Teachers' Union.
Ah! Were you teaching here in New York then?

No, I was a school social worker. I was then. But I wasn't sure I was going to come back and I had a rich friend who had leased a villa in St. Tropez and invited all his friends over. So I went over and did a little singing and met Bud. Because, you know, I've always been interested in music.
They just, my family just said, no, no, no to show business. No, no, you get your degrees and you do that on the side, if necessary.
Where did you get your degrees?

Hunter ... (inaudible). Anyway, (I don't agree with that doctorate.)? (inaudible falsehood?). I don't know what I'd do with it. I just have to do video now with my crazy net video audience. I'm going around doing as much as I can on video tapes.
Well I watched you with the equipment the other night and I think something happened to it.
(Well that was Billy's?). As a matter of fact, he borrowed it and it didn't work.
It was just the way it was all set up, (unintelligible) planning for days and something is wrong with the equipment.

There are of course such fundamental things that are very familiar to you but that other people years and years later will want to know about. I happen to know that you somehow made your way into the United States from Canada. Do you want to go back to Canada and talk about your background there and family and that sort of thing as much as you want? You were born in Canada weren't you?
Yes, I was, yes.
Where specifically?
Toronto.
And when?
And you stayed there in school until when? Were you a kind of drop-out in the days when they weren't using the word?
No.
No, oh.
I started school when I was eight at Nelson British (NelsonBridge, Columbia?).
At where, NelsonBridge
Then we came to (Spokane) Washington.
Now when you say 'we'?
My mother.
Your mother. What about your father?
Well my father is dead. But I had some step-fathers. Mama was married five times.
(LAUGHTER). I was quite fascinated by you saying some step-fathers. (LAUGHTER).
Well I had some brothers and sisters which I never knew because they were born before me and a couple of them died before I was born. (Mother was about 45 before I was born?).
Well, was she in show business or..... No?
No, she just had the wanderlust. Worked her way across
Canada into Washington, Idaho. And my step-father was a miner, so we lived in Idaho and Montana, Washington and Oregon and California in mining towns. And my mother was, let's see, she cooked mostly.
She'd answer an ad in the paper for..... ......
In restaurants or private homes or what? Private homes?
In private homes usually on a farm. I remember a farm and lumber camps and things like that.

And we did that until we moved to Stockton I think. Then my mother became a cook, really; she still cooked but she took care of children more then than she had before. Before that she was a cook mainly. She did have some (unintelligible)
She would have to be up at three o'clock in the morning to get the thing started before they all came into the beanary to eat. The wagons the (unintelligible ?). It was that kind of a life.
Which hardly seems
conducive to the kind of person that you finally became. When did you then first notice the spark of the .........
In highschool.
In highschool which was where?
In Berkeley. There's where I first knew .........
You just really didn't realise that you were musically inclined before that?
My mother had a mandolin that she'd play and she used to carry around with her. But .........
And you didn't pay much attention even to that did you say?
No.
Well does this suggest then that something of the spark of your musicality came from your mother? Did you know anything about any particular talent your father had?
No. Just that (Unintelligible - inaudible)
Oh those were the days
when the mandolin and banjo was a popular home instrument, yes. And just about everybody was trying to work out a fret or two, huh?
(LAUGHTER).
The music is the same as it is now. A lot of the Country Western music is Now its electric, but the same. The style and sound of the singers and lots of the sounds are almost the same.
Now, at this highschool in Berkeley, you did say......
I met some friends who were buying jazz records
Do you remember what some of the first records were?
Louis Armstrong.
Oh, as they would say now, that turned you on, huh? (LAUGHTER).
Yeah....
Did you have a Victrola as they called it then, at home?
Yeah, the crank-up kind.
Yes, yes, uhu. And was there anybody in the house who helped you to see what your potential was in high school?
No, only the records.
So then that accounts in large measure for the fact that you (are self-taught ), is that right?
Yes.

I'd love to hear you talk a little bit about that because even though I've had some training in music, I'm not a composer or a professional musician. I've a PhD in literature and I'm a theater historian, but my work crosses the lines. But anyway, although I read music, I certainly don't place myself in your category or anywhere near it. (LAUGHTER).

But what I'm simply saying is that last night I was looking at Leonard Feather's book which I don't think very much of in many ways, but I was looking at his notations and the bars in which he was showing, in the passages in which he was showing how a jazz musician could understand the horizontal line, whereas the classical musician would have difficulty because he is used to looking at the vertical line.
And I realise that if I had to start now, that I don't think I'd be able to deal with what I was looking at last night.
What book was that?
Leonard Feather's Encyclopedia of Jazz.
Oh, it's got (me in it?).
You are in it!
I know, but I didn't know it had any actual music in it.
Oh yes, yes, yes. It does.
..........something that Leonard wrote. It says when you were born and all that..........
Oh yes, right.
I have a lot.....
You have that.
I have a lot of that, but you see we need it on tape and I'd much rather have it come from you than simply to read into it what somebody else has written.
For instance, what you've just told us here gives us an insight into your background which
I have not read anywhere else. And as a matter of fact, Joe Thomas I think his name is, who was at the concert Sunday, said to me ......
Who's Joe Thomas?
Isn't his name........ Bill Thomas, Bill Thomas isn't it? Yes.
It may be J.C.
Oh, that's it. All these Thomases, yes.
I don't know what those initials stand for........
Who has a card. Yes, he has a card on which he describes himself as 'renaissance man for rent'. (LAUGHTER).
Is that what it said on his card?
Yes. (LAUGHTER).
He gave me his card but I didn't read it. He was handing them out to everyone.
But anyway he sent to me the very next day a copy of the article which he had written about you. There's no indication
as to what periodical it appeared in, but nevertheless, I do have the article.
A newspaper, I think it was (serial?).
The New York, The Herald, it was a paper around for a while. I don't know if it still exists. A Sunday, every Sunday or maybe even every other.
I used to read his (column) but I never did ever read (this card inaudible ?).
I thought you might want to read this about geographic (pictures on a ?) luxurious montage. In 1912 he was .........
I think you might read that speak a little bit louder.
Oh, I keep forgetting you're on tape. Oh no, I........
Oh no, go ahead, do that, do that.
Well I thought I would check it with Gil, I mean .........
That's okay, go ahead.
Because he can react to something........

In 1912 the new born son of a doctor in Toronto. A few years later he took the name of his step-father Evans. His childhood was divided between Ontario, British Columbia and the States of Washington and California.
(TAPE IS TEMPORARILY DISCONTINUED AT THIS POINT).
Both parents trying to.....
Yes, you had this syndrome by ( ?). Your mother had it too. (LAUGHTER).

But this seems to suggest then that after your father's death your mother fell on rather hard times if after being a doctor's wife she ended up being a cook in mining towns and in ........oh that's......
Well she was very independent, you know. Even though my sister had married the owner of a steamship line in Canada, the, what was it?
Melville
The Melville Steamship Line, and so.......
They all married rich.

They married rich and everything, but my mother was very independent which didn't...... She had a falling out with her daughter and her daughter never did help, until we met her one time about twelve years ago I guess.
The 'phone rang one day and this woman Call Evans, said, hello, and she said, well I believe I'm your sister. She came over and it turned out she was my sister. And I never met her before.
Oh! So actually.......

I went to visit her out in Toronto. She also had married a, this was her second marriage. That was the one who had married the steamship man. And now she's married to a salt mine millionaire who was also a very peculiar number. But she died that next year. I had a two week visit with her. I had all kinds of things I wanted to ask her about, you know....
The family.
Because they weren't from Toronto. My father was from Australia. And they came—I was born in Toronto, but I was, my mother was pregnant with me on the way over and they
came from, they came from ( ?).
Yes, that's the kind of thing. Because now, I do want your mother's name and your father's name. You see we want as much of this documentation as we can get. So what was her name originally?
Julia McConechy.
McConey. MONICKY or what?
McCONECHY.
I thought it would be something different. (LAUGHTER).
Well that's a different spelling.
Yes, yes, yes, uhu. Well now, where did your father come from?
I have a niece, who is my sister's daughter. She and I are about the same age. I was born about the same time that my mother's daughter had her baby too. The same time in Canada.
And you're 62 now aren't you?
Yes. She's about that age
now. She had married, this niece of mine, married the man who owned Ash Records. You know, there used to be a jazz label called Ash (Records?).

He was a millionaire. He always ( the fact that he was a millionaire?). Then she married another man in Pennsylvania after that and she lives there somewhere, but I never really have been able to contact her.
Well your family lines are very sketchy then? Very, very sketchy.
My brother lives in San Jose. I met him I think twice.
Was he a full brother?
No, he was a half brother. We all have different fathers. They were born, my sister was born, she was born I think in India. or It may have been Africa, I forget which.
My brother was born in New Zealand. My mother was married when she was fifteen the first time. She was married the second time when she was seventeen.
And Gil was born when she was 45 or something like that.
So actually she is the one you should be writing about. She had the life, I didn't have the life, she had the life.
Well I think that this an is/absolutely fascinating part of your background. And much about your mother is certainly legitimate. This is what..... or was it illegitimate uh? (LAUGHTER).

Because one of the aspects of being able to talk at least five hours here is that we do get a chance to bring out some things which one doesn't ordinarily get a chance to talk about. Some things that are inside that he really wants to explore. As I've said, these ridiculous tape shows that we look at so often on how did you get started and that sort of thing, is not what we are about. And they don't end up being very, very valuable at all.

But I think this kind of thing is because it gives us an insight into various kinds of social backgrounds. And here, we are particularly involved in what happened to a family that migrated from Australia.
I think your mother must have been a very beautiful woman or something to, you know, have acquired such an assortment of husbands including a doctor.
She was really a flirt you know. She flirted when she ninety. She was still flirting, right? And men were still proposing to her.
Oh dear. How old was she when she died?
She was around ninety.
And what year was that?
Well over the period of years, were you in close touch with her?
Well the last few years she was living with my brother. He was in San Jose. He went and got her. She was living in (Balboa?) by herself. He felt like she shouldn't be living by herself.
Balboa, California?
But it didn't turn out to be such a good idea I don't really think. But I was attending ( ) so I couldn't do
anything about it. So my brother took her to San Jose and she lived there until she died.

She could only really, she could only go on doing what she wanted to do. Like the same thing, what she wanted to do, she didn't want to be cooped up like that in a house, you know. But she didn't have the where-withal that's all that mattered... that was the matter. If She had money she could have gone on and traveling. ?). She liked to do that.
In those days it took like six months to go from South Africa to India to Australia, I mean really those (British Isles?) people really got around ......
Oh yes, they'd lose a rudder and.....
They'd lose a rudder?
Yes, they'd lose a rudder on the boat. She drifted once on an ocean liner. It might take a month or more between New Zealand and Durban at that time.
Oh, incredible. I was going to say another thing is that ten years ago

we were much less enlightened about geriatrics than we are now. And I would certainly say that since most of my work involves theater people and musicians who are anywhere from 75 which eliminates you, but from 75 to 96 years old I have come to know a great deal, to learn a great deal, about older people.
I was telling you about Rudolph (Bremwald?). Did you hear about him? He's fantastic. I saw a picture of him in that High Fidelity magazine. He's ninety years old?
Yes.
Very spry. A full head of black hair, right?

That's fantastic. And Lee Whipper (Dr. Ripley) is 96. And the only thing that slows him down, I've just talked to him today, the actor, and the only thing that slows him down is his eyesight and that doesn't slow him down too much. But I've really learned a great deal about them.
Eubie Blake too.
What, Eubie's 89.

and he's in Germany right now. Doing a concert. In West Germany, a jazz concert in West Germany. He sailed on 22nd October. Yes. But I want to get back to this business of your teaching yourself for a minute.

And we haven't finished talking about your mother, but we started out and let it go and I think I would like to sort of get back to that and then we can get back to the statistics at another point because I think it has a lot to do with how you moved up, let us say, in the music world. And I think that these early origins are as important as anything we can talk about.
So, when you say you taught yourself, how did you actually go about learning how to read music? You had absolutely no, not even in school you had any help, is that it?

I still can't read music too well, you know. I'm like what you call semi-literate in music. And I really never did practice reading music. I can write music for other people, to play you know. But to read other people's music, I'm not too quick at it.
His eyes aren't too great
either. That had to have something to do with it. Well my eyesight is, my close-up eyesight is bad. But that really doesn't ......
But do you wear corrective glasses? Oh yes.

I never had the inclination to learn to read very much. Although at one time I had to go to the library all the time to pick the scores out you know, and read them. That's how I learned about orchestration and arranging.
Now that's what I want you to talk about a little bit here. I think that's extremely difficult.

That's the ( ?), library. It's not really hard though. Because I mean, if you know what you want. It's the same thing as going to school to learn it. You simply go and get it and learn it. If you hear it on record and want to know how it's done, if the score is available you go and get it. If the score is not available, then you copy the record yourself. You know, and just play it over and over again until you get every note of it.

That's how I learned really to arrange and how I learned to read really. And to write the notes down was by listening to the record and then painstakingly putting down on paper what I heard on the records, you know.
At first it was slow and after that it gradually (it got to where I?) could do it readily. But that was my first arrangement, I know it was a copy off a record.

As it happens now, the young people they (bottom?) for me to buy the records and listen to them and the next day they've got it down. You know, they finger it instrumentally or in a few days I've got it written down. It's always been like that really.

I mean when you say you're self-taught you really don't mean that you learned all by yourself without any help. I got all the help of everybody I ever heard play. And all the writing I ever wanted to read I got from the library to see how it was done, you know. So I really had to learn from .........
So you would take out books on composition and orchestration and that sort of thing?

Oh yes. I had to know at least ( ?). I may be going back to the library one of these days. It's funny, in this Country, you know, when you show your library card for identification they laugh at you. They want your driver's license, right?
That's right.

But I mean, why wouldn't an up-to-date library card be alright? It should be. In a sensible setup it would be. But here where it's not like that. You have to have a car. You have to own some property in order to be identified.
That's right. That's right.
And gee, I'm afraid some people even get mad at me or go into gales of laughter when I offer that as identification.
And of course it's a statement isn't it? It's a statement. Because we can think of cultural atmospheres in which this ought to be a very significant indication of the kind of person.
Sure. An up-to-date card you've gone along with them, where you know, you've paid your dues and whatever
it is for the library card (and it should be an identification card?).

How can they expect anybody in Manhattan to have a driver's license or a car when there's no place to park it, that's the one that always gets me. (What do you mean, you don't have (You really don't need a driver's license?)
That's right. Well I gave up on mine after my car had been stolen four times (LAUGHTER). Four times.

Anita sold hers before it got stolen. I've got so tired going out and moving it in the morning. And the battery will be dead and the acid will spill on the front of my clothes and burn them. It turns so cold in New York.
We've lived in this neighborhood all this time. The children were born on 15th Street.
Oh really? Where?
We've been here five years in a brownstone and we bounced all on 15th Street, what was the address, 125?
Where were you married and under what circumstances?
The West Village. We never got out of the village.
Well, I meant at home or were you married in a church?
It was in an apartment. We looked up a minister in the phone books.
Yes, we thought we could find one within walking distance. (LAUGHTER).
On No. 2 Bank Street. And it turned out to be a peculiar coincidence. He was 75, he was 76 and his wife was 55. It was like the same kind of difference between our ages.
Between the two of you. Well I must tell you at a time I might have been aghast at that but as I said, I've learned so much about old men I am no longer aghast. (LAUGHTER). Do you remember his name?
He gave us a ......
A certificate?
An all-American kind of Presbyterian name.
And he said we've got to have a whole lot of happiness, you know. That kind of Spanish. There he was, with all his kids around. They were attendants.
That's right, the children were .........
And who was your first wife? Do you want to say a little bit about that?
It was funny, I said how much do I owe you? And he said, well whatever you think your wife is worth, put that one on me, right? (LAUGHTER). I think I gave him ten, because it's all I could afford.
None of that two dollar stuff.
Yes, it's been a long time story huh? Well now, did you, that looks as though it might be a later style wedding ring. Is that the one you actually married with?
No, we got these in a little jewelery store next to the Vanguard. What did we have at first, plain ones didn't we?
Yes plain. They were round gold ones.
Plain round gold ones, yes.
Yes, but this wasn't expensive, they are much more jolly.
Yes, yes.
( ?) scope and his is like musical bars.
This was twenty-five dollars, but it's cute.

It's the first ring I've really had for a long time. Because my mother bought me one once when she went to work in (Yellowstone?) National Park when I was living in Butte, Montana. I stayed there with my step-father who was working the mines and my mother took a cooking job in (Gardner?) which is the entrance to Yellowstone National Park. And she brought me back a greatest ring. It was silver and it had a black onyx top with two silver bears standing on their hind legs. (LAUGHTER). I left it in a, I left it in a hotel I think. ( ?).
How old were you? About?
About ten.
Oh.
He told me that she said, Buster don't forget the mandolin. That was his job to remember the mandolin whenever they moved.
And now we've come up with a family nickname too, huh, Buster. What do you call him?
Gil. Or Peach.
People used to call me that
and my mother didn't know who they were asking for. She remembered that my name was Gil. She named me as Gilmore... different names.
Did you ever have any aspirations for going to college?
Well no, my mother wanted me to go. But by the time I was through highschool I had a band.
Oh!

And as a matter of fact, this summer when we came back from Tokyo through the Hawaiian Islands I met (fellows?) that we used to have a band together in Stockton thirty five years ago. (inaudible) ... clothing store.
Yes. Did you pull members of your band from fellows who were already out or some of your highschool classmates?
Yes, that's right, you know, people who lived around there in the area. Not necessarily from the same highschool, but from towns nearby.
And in what kind of places did you play in those days?
Summer resorts. We played Lake Tahoe, places like that. (And balls?).
Were you doing anything with your own music at that point?
A little bit. I was writing a few things. little
Do you remember the first thing that you wrote?

Mostly. (unintelligible) Well yes, Ned and, this fellow told you about... I scored out songs. He and I wrote some things together. We were trying to remember how they went. We couldn't remember, we could remember the titles but we couldn't remember how they went. (LAUGHTER).
Which means you don't have those (the articles?) of early manuscripts around any more?
I lost all those. I left those at, I left those at Skinny [Ennis's] basement you know. (unintelligible) There was nowhere else to store them, so I scored them there.
I read somewhere that your band was active at Modesto College in California, that it started there in Modesto.
That started there.......
That's the only place I went to college, in Augusta, Georgia. Modesto
How long did you stay there?
Two years. And I worked in the day, I had a daytime job. I had some dates sometimes. (LAUGHTER).
There is a history if you let me assemble it somewhere. (LAUGHTER).
We got a job in Santa Cruz and we went down there in Monterey in California.
And how big was that band?
And from there we went down to Balboa.
How big of a group did you have and what did you have with you?
I had four saxophones. I started out with three saxophones, and three brass and we added one more of each and we had twelve, in Balboa.
We stayed in Balboa for three years.
Oh really?
Yes. Then there was no business, nothing was happening, so this man wanted to get a band together and he contacted me through
MCA. Skinny Ennis
Now what were those three years that you, the dates of the three years that you in Moersto? Is that on there?
You know, I must stop you for just one moment because I heard you say you have to go to the store. So.......
It wasn't until 4.30 though was it?
We are not going to have any food left.
Oh, you're not going to have any food left? (LAUGHTER).
I've looked around and there's something for everybody to eat except me so I don't feel as panicky about it, except tomorrow.
(TAPE IS DISCONTINUED TEMPORARILY)
( ) was apparently famous there because in what, 1966, he did something at, a concert at Casa Mesa, California, South of Los Angeles.
Just a few miles from Balboa. And I had lived there.

And you worked there, but you worked there about eight years during the 30s and lo and behold, they all came out you know, it was amazing, he hadn't been there in thirty years. And they remembered him from all that time.
It's strange to see a lady thirty years later. (LAUGHTER). They were only girls...
If ( / are the same inside ?) they'd say, wow, how that girl grew up. (LAUGHTER).
( ?) she was on the way to Spain. Is that where she was honey, on the way to Spain?
Or Uruguay or both.
Oh that's right, she had to fly to Uruguay too, to a hospital.
In the lab?
The lab yes. ( like the nasty hassles, like you might have, she went back into business .... and kind of cooled out.
Were you any more financially successful when you were married to
We survived.
She was like an Andrews sister though, so that might have helped. When I saw her I felt, wow, she looks like Patty Andrews, I remember. All done up (broad center?).
Yes.
Was she a singer?
She had been a singer, yes. She was from Philadelphia.
And what was her name?
Lilian Grace.
GRACE?
Yes.
And how long were you married?
Ten years.
From when to when?
Eleven I think. '50 to '60 from '50 to '61.
Was that an instant romance too?
No. No it wasn't. She was married to a saxophone player in Claude Thornhill's
orchestra and I worked with Claude Thornhill and I met her when I was playing and I with [him]

Oh, so you met her first when you were both connected with the orchestra in some way? But you had nothing to do with the fact that she was no longer married to the saxophone player I take it? (LAUGHTER).
No.
What was it like working for Thornhill?

It was a fine workshop for me. It was a full orchestra which is not easy to get to you know, to work to unless you are at school, for that. We had a french horn, two french horns, two trombones, two trumpets, five saxophones, three flutes, a tuba and a piano, drums, bass, guitar, bass. So it was a great opportunity for me to, uh...

Through Skinny Ennis this man who had the band in California, I met Claude Thornhill and I was sent to him to write for the orchestra. Skinny [Ennis] had one of those managers you know, who would sit back
and twirl his moustache and say, 'who is the greatest arranger in the World, the vocal arranger in the World?'
Claree Thornhill
At that particular time California had a 'Loch Lomond,' hit record out with Maxine Sullivan, and we had made an arrangement for her.
Oh yes.

The villain being what been injected to you by the culture, by the outside institutions. And that's the basis of our schizophrenia that had been injected into us by the outside world to keep what's inside of us from coming out.

first brutalized into this condition of so-called civilization. He thought that you would get more out of it, physically so ( I would go and we would have breathing sessions. Then there's a thing called the gag reflex which is something that's really not too well known. But it's a fantastic therapy, a medicine. It's not easy to do and hardly anyone knows about it, but the gag reflex is an automatic gagging. The word gag is wrong because you don't gag when the gag reflex occurs. It's an involuntary free release from your waist, from your groin right out through your mouth.

So when you do it, it's right before you have a meal so there's nothing in your stomach and you by-pass that totally. So when you exhale you go .....ah.... And when you do that and especially when you first do it, the first few months when you do it, the anger that you have pinned down there you know,
ever since when, all of a sudden it roars out of you you know. And you feel a direct opening in the gag reflex. It's a pleasurable feeling which accompanies it.

It was discovered accidentally in a clinic. A men was doing clinical work for thirty years and a man came in one day/he started unloading this enger, this way. He started....ah... and he got so healthy right after the session and he got so cured from it temporarily until it built up again, that the man began to look into it, to find out if it was a natural medical thing to do.

And it's hard to do because you live in a culture where you've got people around you and you're afraid, like if you take a breath and you go like that because you know that when it comes free, at first if it doesn't come free you will gag, you go ....ah.... and it stops.

But if it doesn't stop and it goes ...ah.... you will make a scream and you think all the neighbors will come and they'll call the police. So you've got all this paranoia naturally, so it's hard to do, you know. But if you can do that it helps. So that was part of my therapy, long xfxex answer to the question you asked. And that's all supported by the individual family which echoes that same thing to their children because they don't want their neighbors to think that they're different, right?
That's right.

So there's no way, in this particular set up that civilization has now, we can't say that thing should be changed like that because it would cause havoc. That's the problem. To try to raise a child, let a child raise itself in a natural self- regulatory manner, could lead to havoc. In a neighborhood or household or state or whatever, whatever the situation is, is based on this other particular anti-life type of situation.
All organised things that belong to us, personal, private things that shouldn't belong to
anybody but us and have been organised to the public thing like religion and a notion and democracy.
And pregnancy. (LAUGHTER).

Nations not based on the work you do but democracy, based on the little man. The authoritarian family and echoes the state and does all those things to you and misrepresents to you in an innocent or even if it's calculated manner, they do it because it has to be done.

Parents for instance, they say, well this has to be done. You must do that. For example, the mother says to the child, you're a certain age now, you can no longer associate with that person because you have a life to lead now.
That's right, yes.
Is that the way you were brought up?
Yes.

I had a guy tell me that his mother, said his mother took him and the boys that he grew up with, his friends, who worked for the family, they were rich and lived in ( ? ). He was an arranger with Claude Thornhill, he got drafted and I replaced him. The

mother said, now you can take these boys over to the, to New York and go to Radio City and show them the whole town like that and when you come home you're not going to stay with them or speak to them. And the man said to me, he said, my mother wasn't prejudice. (LAUGHTER). Do you believe that? Do you believe that? That's what happened.

I had a student tell me at York College where I teach that when she was a little girl walking down the street with her mother, when her mother saw a negro passing by, she would turn and point and she would say to the child, you're not supposed to like that.

Another style on that was Anita told me they used to each them on Staten Island they've lived there three hundred years, the family, her mother's side of the family. And they always lived in Staten Island which is a mixture there. And her mother would take them to 125th Street they would both burst out crying, they never saw so many black people in their lives. It scared them. Scared by them. That's another angle. All depends on your conditioning.
Yes. I came up in York, Pennsylvania which was certainly a white city. And there were very few negroes there. And I certainly did not live in a negro neighborhood. There were just two

negro families for blocks around and we were in an upper middle class neighborhood which had white doctors and that sort of thing. And then we were just on the fringe of this two or three block of extremely rich white neighborhood.

And my father and mother used to drive down to Princess Street which was the main drag for negroes on Saturday night. And we would sit there in the car and watch people. And that would be our entertainment. And I remember when I was eighteen years old and this is your interview and not mine, but I really want to comment on what you were just saying, that when I was eighteen years old I went to Philadelphia to work in a beauty parlor once one summer because I was trained in a prep school where I took a trade.

And I wrote my first letter home and I said, oh mother, I didn't know there were so many negroes in the world. So I can fully understand what Anita was saying. It's difficult for everybody to understand.
It's conditioning.
But those of us who came up that way.......
It's a simple thing to understand too. If you observe your children or anybody to see

what conditioning does. How you like this thing because it's familiar, even if it's terrible or you know. It's so simple to understand. People go through such terrible droves of anger and guilt and all kinds of emotions like that because of theirs or other people's conditioning which is based on it.

All you can do is figure out what it is and either cope with it or go around it. It isn't always easy to do but at least you can get around some of it. Even say right out what it is and get that straightened out or if it looks like an impossible situation, try to be lucky enough to be the artful dodger. (LAUGHTER).
